Schneider Electric SE (SU-FR) · Investment memo · 7 November 2026

Schneider Electric: operating profit will beat consensus, EPS will land 6 to 7% below consensus first, and 2027 is the cleaner year of a two-year holding

For Richard, 7 November 2026. Prices are at the close of 23 October 2026, the price used by the model and the dashboard. The next company data point is the FY2026 results and FY2027 guidance on 18 February 2027. Data definitions are in the end notes.

Schneider at a glance: a EUR 137bn group in its strongest growth year, with its shares 26% below their 52-week high.

#0 Summary: key insights, implications and conclusions

The bottom line. Schneider's FY2027 operating profit is largely booked, but FY2027 consensus EPS is 6 to 7% too high because it has not absorbed the new shares and debt that fund the PTC acquisition. The per-share evidence will therefore worsen before it improves, while the operating evidence keeps improving. The window in which both turn positive together opens between the February 2027 results and the July 2027 results.

The business. Schneider is the world's largest focused electrical-distribution and energy-management group, with EUR 40bn of 2025 revenue (Energy Management about 83%, Industrial Automation 17%). It is number one or two in the activities that carry almost all of its growth, and it is the most specified power vendor inside data centres.

The moment. Schneider is in the strongest demand environment of its modern history. Organic growth has stepped up from 8.9% in 2025 to 16.9% in Q3 2026, data-centre orders grew at triple-digit rates in both Q2 and Q3 2026, and a new insider chief executive has reset pricing, productivity and cash discipline. In October 2026 Schneider announced the largest acquisition in its history, PTC (USD 23.7bn enterprise value), funded with 25m new shares and EUR 16bn of debt. The shares have fallen about 26% from their high while earnings estimates rose.

The case, in eight points.

1Operations

Schneider's operating story is strong, mechanical and largely booked. Data-centre systems ordered in Q2 and Q3 2026 convert into revenue over 12 to 24 months, so most FY2027 revenue is already in the backlog. The 2026 price increases carry over into H1 2027, while input costs annualise more slowly, and revenue is outgrowing a near-frozen overhead. Our FY2027 forecasts of 10.5% organic growth and a 20.5% adjusted EBITA margin need nothing that Schneider has not demonstrated in the last four quarters. We put the probability that FY2027 revenue lands within 5% of our base at about 75%, and the same probability for adjusted EBITA at about 70%.

2Per share

Schneider's per-share story is 6 to 7% weaker than consensus, for reasons already on the public record. FY2027 carries a full year of the 25m new shares (4.3% more shares), only one quarter of PTC profit, and a first EUR 6bn of acquisition debt priced at 4.3% against the 3.5% assumed in most broker models. Our FY2027 EPS is EUR 11.76 against consensus of EUR 12.61, even though our net income is within 1% of consensus. The share count explains the gap: consensus EPS implies about 555m shares, while the real count is about 591m. "Beat on operations, miss on EPS" is the most likely FY2027 pattern, as it was in FY2025.

3Sequence

The order in which estimates move matters more than where they end. FY2027 EPS consensus should drift down 3 to 5% across the December 2026 and February 2027 consensus collections, while EBITDA consensus edges up. The first clearly positive EPS revisions should arrive with the H1 2027 results in late July 2027, when the price carry-over peaks and a guidance raise is most likely; we put the probability of a raise during 2027 at about 65%. The headline revision series and the dashboard's sell-side momentum letter (B today) will therefore look worse before they look better.

4Multiple

Schneider's multiple is being set by its sector, not by Schneider. The electrification basket explains half to two-thirds of the variance in Schneider's share price. That basket is de-rating on the financing of the AI build-out (the four large hyperscalers' free cash flow has fallen from about USD 60bn to about USD 7bn, and neocloud credit is under strain), on interest rates and on a risk-off rotation; all 16 stocks in the dashboard's sector carry a technical momentum grade of D or F. The company-specific discount that opened in October 2026 is for PTC and capital allocation, and that discount is the part that delivery can close.

5Valuation

Schneider's shares are cheap against their last five years, not against their last ten. On our EPS the shares trade at about 17.7 to 18.2 times two-year-forward earnings, which is the 25th percentile of five years but close to the ten-year median of 17.6x. FactSet's 16.3x rests on consensus EPS that has not absorbed the new shares, and the dashboard's 21.3x is a trailing multiple made stale by the earnings inflection.

6Return

The return at the guideline fair multiple comes from earnings, not from re-rating. Viewforth's guideline multiple for a Bottoming stock is 15.34x, the 30th percentile of ten years. At that multiple the model gives +5.2% to December 2027, almost all of it dividends, and +24.4% to June 2029 (+8.5% a year), because EPS compounding at about 15% a year outruns a 16% de-rating from today's multiple. Each turn of multiple above the guideline is worth about EUR 15 a share (6.6%); at the ten-year median the 18-month return is about +20%.

7Skew

The skew is positive on operating outcomes and negative on per-share consensus and sentiment. The positive skew lies in FY2026 landing at the top of guidance, the year-end backlog, an FY2027 organic guide set above the midpoint of the 7% to 10% framework, the H1 2027 margin, and the 2030 margin framework being beaten. The negative skew lies in FY2027 EPS consensus; in the 2028 growth debate, when data-centre normalisation, the competitor capacity wave, full PTC consolidation and the interest on EUR 16bn all land together; and in sentiment towards anything debt-financed in the AI supply chain.

8Setup

The case fits the "demand-driven earnings power step-up" setup, with a fresh cause for concern attached. Structural demand is moving EPS growth from a 7% CAGR (2019 to 2025) to about 15% (2025 to 2030). The PTC deal, peak leverage in 2027 and a buyback pause until 2029 keep the setup from being crisp. The one risk that would turn a deceleration into a decline, a financing-led pause in data-centre orders, sits outside the company's disclosure and would hit 2028 earnings, not 2027.

Implication. Schneider is a high-quality compounder in a peak operating year. Its share price is behaving like the capital-allocation underperformance archetype, while its earnings behave like the outperformance archetype. The forecast question is therefore not whether the operating profit arrives; it is how much of that profit reaches each share, and when the market stops pricing the sector's financing fear into Schneider's multiple. In practice, the operating evidence will keep improving through July 2027, the per-share and sentiment evidence will get worse first, and the window in which both turn together opens between the February 2027 results and the expected July 2027 guidance raise.

Scorecard

The case is strongest on forecast growth and the operating environment, and weakest on the return at the guideline multiple and the near-term scope for upgrades.

The five judgements that move the value most over the next one to two years, with the arithmetic

All the arithmetic below uses our FY2027 base: revenue of EUR 51.0bn, adjusted EBITA of EUR 10.2bn (a 20.5% margin), a 24.3% tax rate, about 591m average shares and EPS of EUR 11.76. On that base, one point of adjusted EBITA margin is worth about EUR 510m, and EUR 100m of EBITA after tax is worth about EUR 0.13 of EPS (1.1%).

Currency, net price-cost and the share count each move FY2027 EPS by 4 to 7%, and one turn of the multiple moves the value more than any operating line.

Judgement 1: FY2027 organic growth of 10.5%, and the overhead loop that depends on it.

  • Each point of organic growth is worth about 1% of EPS. One point of organic growth is EUR 453m of revenue. At a 20% to 25% drop-through it adds EUR 90m to 115m of EBITA (Bernstein's EUR 90m per point sits at the low end of that range, and 2026's incremental margins at the high end), which is EUR 70m to 85m after tax and EUR 0.12 to 0.14 of EPS (about 1.0% to 1.2%).
  • The bear case is a four-point shortfall, to 6.5% organic growth. The bear case combines a financing-led data-centre order pause from early 2027 with short-cycle products rolling over. The shortfall costs EUR 360m to 460m of EBITA and EUR 0.46 to 0.59 of EPS (4% to 5%).
  • The shortfall compounds through the overhead. Support-function costs still grow at about 6% a year, so with revenue growing only 6.5% the support-function ratio stops falling. Our base has that ratio falling 0.7 points (worth about EUR 350m), so losing the fall takes a further EUR 0.3 to 0.4 off EPS. Under-absorption of Schneider's prefabrication capacity, which has grown fourfold, would add to the damage; Eaton lost 100 to 270 basis points of margin for a quarter during its own capacity ramp. Together these effects take bear-case FY2027 EPS to about EUR 10.7 (−9%), with FY2028 EPS at about EUR 11.2.
  • The bull case is a 2.5-point beat, to 13% organic growth. That path, which Morgan Stanley and Redburn model, adds EUR 225m to 290m of EBITA and EUR 0.29 to 0.37 of EPS (+2.5% to +3%). Combined with easing metals prices, the beat gives bull-case FY2027 EPS of about EUR 12.4.

Judgement 2: 2027 is the one clearly net-price-positive year, worth about EUR 400m.

  • Schneider's 2026 price increases annualise faster than its input costs. The 2026 product price increases (1.7%, 3.7% and 5.1% in the first three quarters) annualise into H1 2027. Input costs annualise more slowly, because hedging covers about 20% of the top three commodities and tapers over twelve months, and list-price pass-through takes three to six months. The model credits net price-cost with about 50 basis points of FY2027 margin, net of wage inflation and systems mix, which is two-thirds of the FY2027 margin gain.
  • Zero net price-cost would leave the FY2027 margin flat on 2026. Net price-cost could fall to zero through a renewed copper and silver spike, a wider US tariff (11% of Schneider's employees are in Mexico), or competitor capacity arriving a year early. In that case FY2027 EBITA is EUR 400m lower, EPS is EUR 0.51 lower (−4.4%), and the FY2027 margin is about 19.7%, flat on 2026.
  • Metals are a symmetrical risk. Copper and silver are about 4.5% of revenue. A 10% move in their prices left unrecovered for a year is worth about EUR 230m of EBITA, 45 basis points of margin and EUR 0.29 of EPS (2.5%), in either direction.

Judgement 3: the PTC per-share arithmetic, and when consensus absorbs it.

  • The share count explains almost all of the gap to consensus EPS. Our FY2027 net income of EUR 6,948m over 591m shares gives EPS of EUR 11.76. Consensus net income of EUR 6,995m over the 555m shares implied by consensus EPS gives EUR 12.61. The same consensus net income over 591m shares gives EUR 11.84. The share count alone therefore explains about EUR 0.77 of the EUR 0.85 gap, and it has been a fact, not a forecast, since the prospectus supplement of 21 October 2026.
  • The debt cost is a further, smaller risk. The model carries an average cost of 4.6% on about EUR 16bn of acquisition debt. The first EUR 6bn was priced at 4.3%; the remaining EUR 10bn is to be issued partly in US dollars, where A-rated issuers paid 5.65% to 5.90% in October 2026. Each further 100 basis points on the whole EUR 16bn costs EUR 160m before tax, or EUR 0.20 of EPS (1.5% of FY2028 EPS of EUR 13.51). If only the dollar portion costs 90 basis points more, the effect is about EUR 0.11.
  • The PTC closing date shifts FY2027 EPS by 1% to 1.5%. PTC consolidated from 1 October 2027 contributes about EUR 260m of Q4 2027 EBITA against about EUR 185m of Q4 interest. A slip of one quarter into 2028 would cost 1% to 1.5% of FY2027 EPS and would lower peak leverage.
  • Tax is the offset, and we have left it as a buffer. The model's 24.8% tax rate from 2028 compares with Redburn's estimate of about 23% (PTC's own rate is 21%). The difference is worth up to 2.3% of EPS, and we have deliberately left it in the model as a conservative buffer.

Judgement 4: currency, the biggest single swing factor in EPS.

  • A 10% move in the US dollar moves FY2027 EPS by 4.6%. The US dollar accounts for 38% of revenue, and translation exposure is unhedged. A 10% move in the dollar changes revenue by EUR 1,505m and adjusted EBITA by EUR 427m (a 28% drop-through), which is EUR 323m after tax and EUR 0.55 of EPS.
  • Brokers' currency paths imply a small headwind against the model. The model assumes a neutral currency effect in FY2027 (positive in H1, negative in H2) at about 1.17 EUR/USD. Brokers' paths of 1.16 to 1.20 by mid-2027 imply a 1% to 1.5% EPS headwind if the dollar weakens 2% to 3% from the model's rate.
  • Currency, not volume, has the larger record of moving EPS. Currency is what took FY2025 EPS consensus from EUR 9.77 down to the outcome of EUR 8.59, in a year when organic delivery beat expectations.

Judgement 5: the multiple, which is worth more than any operating line.

  • The guideline multiple gives +5.2% to December 2027. At 31 December 2027 the model values the shares at 15.34x two-year-forward EPS (FY2029 EPS of EUR 15.21), which is EUR 233 a share; adding EUR 10.2 of dividends received gives EUR 243.40, a return of +5.2%. Each 1.0x of multiple is worth EUR 15.2 a share, 6.6% of today's price.
  • Other multiples change the 18-month return far more than any operating judgement. At my central fair multiple of 16.5x (see #11) the value is EUR 261 including dividends (+13%); at the ten-year median of 17.6x, EUR 278 (+20%); at the 75th percentile of 21.0x, EUR 330 (+42%). At the ten-year 10th percentile of 12.6x the value is EUR 202 on base EPS (−13%) and EUR 168 on bear FY2029 EPS of about EUR 12.5 (−27%).
  • Over three years the same arithmetic is more generous. To June 2029, the guideline multiple gives EUR 287.85 (+24.4%), and the ten-year median gives about EUR 328 (+42%, about 14% a year). The multiple matters most, and it is the driver that the company controls least over 18 months.

1Operating environment: tailwinds, and the headwinds that qualify them

Two structural demand drivers are running at once, and both are backed by orders. A short-cycle recovery is layered on top of them.

Data centres. Data centres account for about 30% of Schneider's sales on Redburn's measure, and Schneider's data-centre orders grew at triple-digit rates in Q2 and Q3 2026. US hyperscaler capex is up about 45% in 2026. Management says its visibility extends into 2028 and guides to a 12% to 14% data-centre revenue CAGR to 2030; data-centre growth in 2026 alone (+25% to 30%) is far above that guide.

Grid. Grid investment is an independent second driver. US investor-owned utilities propose at least USD 1.4 trillion of capex over five years, and European network capex is growing 10% to 12% a year. The EU F-gas Regulation bans sulphur hexafluoride (SF6) insulating gas in new medium-voltage switchgear from January 2026, with further steps in 2028, 2030 and 2032. SF6-free switchgear is 10% to 15% dearer, and Schneider already achieves an 80% substitution rate.

Short-cycle recovery. After a 2025 destocking trough, Schneider's product growth stepped up from 9% in Q1 2026 to 13% in Q2 and 17% in Q3, and distributors' purchases from Schneider and their sales to end customers are in balance.

Backlog and peers. Schneider's backlog was EUR 25.4bn (+18%) at end-2025, and management described it as "another record" at the end of Q3 2026. Peers confirm that the cycle is sector-wide: ABB Electrification's orders rose 70% in Q3 2026 with a 1.4x book-to-bill, Vertiv's orders rose more than 100%, and Eaton has completed 18 of its 24 capacity projects.

Six headwinds qualify the tailwinds, and each has a date. The table summarises when each headwind bites and what it acts on; the detail follows.

The fundamental headwinds bite from late 2027 onwards; only the financing fear acts now, and it acts on the multiple rather than on 2027 earnings.

HeadwindEvidenceWhen it bitesActs on

2Financing of the demandHyperscaler free cash flow about USD 60bn → 7bn; CoreWeave credit default swaps about 1,140 basis points; USD 260bn of US projects cancelled in 2026Now on the multiple; orders first, revenue 12–24 months laterThe multiple now; 2028 revenue
3Conversion frictionTexas permit pause; New York one-year moratorium; Virginia SB 843 freeze proposed from July 20272026–2027Timing between quarters

1. Competitor capacity will erode Schneider's pricing from late 2027. Bernstein counts about USD 6bn of competitor capacity ramping over 18 months, including Eaton's USD 1.5bn across 24 North American sites, while LS Electric and Shanghai Liangxin are entering US data-centre switchgear with products certified by Underwriters Laboratories (UL). Benchmark US switchgear lead times have already fallen from 60 to 40 weeks. Morgan Stanley's distributor survey shows the share of distributors receiving supplier price increases falling from 68% in Q2 to 54% in Q3 2026, the first observable sign of cooling.

2. The financing of data-centre demand is under strain now. On Jefferies' count, the four large hyperscalers' aggregate free cash flow fell from about USD 60bn in late 2025 to about USD 7bn in mid-2026. Meta is raising USD 95bn. CoreWeave's bonds yield near 15% and its five-year credit default swaps trade around 1,140 basis points, and spreads on data-centre asset-backed securities are at multi-year highs. Heatmap data cited by Morgan Stanley count USD 260bn of planned US data-centre investment cancelled in 2026.

3. Permitting friction moves revenue between quarters rather than removing it. Texas paused data-centre environmental permits in September 2026 pending an audit of 474 GW of grid-interconnection requests; New York imposed a one-year moratorium on new hyperscale sites; and Virginia bill SB 843 proposes a three-year rezoning freeze from July 2027. These brakes push developers to generate power on site, behind the meter (22% of capacity under construction), and on-site generation raises the electrical content per megawatt that Schneider can supply.

4. Input costs and tariffs are being priced through, but with a lag. In H1 2026 Schneider absorbed EUR 330m of raw-material headwind and EUR 104m of tariff headwind, and gross pricing covered only 65% of the total. Silver rose nearly 100% and copper about 30%.

5. Currency is a continuous drag on reported profit. Currency cut adjusted EBITA by EUR 482m in FY2025 and by EUR 173m in H1 2026.

6. 800-volt direct-current (DC) power is a long-dated threat that will not bite before 2029. 800-volt DC architecture with solid-state transformers threatens traditional alternating-current uninterruptible power supplies (UPS) and switchgear. Secure Power, the Schneider business most exposed, is about a third of data-centre revenue, or roughly 10% of group sales. Adoption will be slow: NVIDIA's Kyber rack platform has slipped to 2028, solid-state transformers cost about 3.5 times conventional equipment, and native DC is expected to be only about 10% of installations by 2030. The hybrid "sidecar" phase before then lifts electrical content per megawatt from about USD 2.5m to over USD 3m. Schneider is positioned for the transition: it has its own solid-state transformer in customer testing, holds the first UL 2140 certification for prefabricated power assemblies, and is a certified partner for NVIDIA's DSX POD reference design.

Inference and so-what. The fundamental environment is the best Schneider has had, and it carries more than two years of order visibility. FY2027 organic growth in the 9% to 12% range is therefore underwritten by orders already booked, whatever happens to new orders. The headwinds that matter for earnings are moderate and dated: price fade from late 2027, and commodity costs that are being priced through. The headwind that matters for the shares right now, the financing of the AI build-out, acts at market level and through the multiple, not through the 18-month revenue line. Hyperscaler and neocloud financing is the one external variable that could turn a deceleration into a decline; because financing acts on orders first and on revenue 12 to 24 months later, its earnings effect is a 2028 question.

Counter-case. The financing crack may already be reaching demand. The Wisdom Library's rule that "a capital-intensive theme cracks at its financing before its demand" is already playing out in credit markets, and Deutsche Bank warns of an "abrupt slowdown in data-centre deployment by 2028". Only 13% of the US data-centre pipeline to 2032 is under construction, and Bernstein counts only 35% of the announced pipeline as credible. If the core hyperscaler customers, and not just the neoclouds, are now debt-financed, a closed debt market in 2027 would reach Schneider's orders within a quarter.

What would change my view. Four signals would change my view: hyperscaler capex guidance cuts in late January and February 2027; ABB's or Vertiv's Q4 book-to-bill falling below 1.0x; the Texas audit or the Virginia vote turning into statewide freezes; and medium-voltage switchgear lead times falling below 35 weeks before mid-2027.

Versus the market. The sell-side is right on the sector risks (the financing of demand and the 2028 pricing fade), and I agree with it. Where I differ is that the market is treating a deceleration in the rate of growth as if it were evidence of a decline in the level of revenue, and the backlog arithmetic does not support that reading for 2027.

Conclusion: the tailwinds are the strongest in the sector and are order-backed for 18 months, the fundamental headwinds are dated to 2028, and the live headwind is a financing fear acting on the multiple rather than on 2027 earnings.

Score: 84, set by the Rater. Several structural, order-backed forces reach a large share of sales at once: data centres (about 30% of sales, triple-digit orders in Q2 and Q3 2026, visibility into 2028), grid capex in the US and Europe, the law-dated EU SF6 phase-out and a short-cycle recovery, taking organic growth from 8.9% to 16.9%; consensus sales growth at the 88th percentile is honest, since peers confirm the cycle. The direct threats are real but dated (about USD 6bn of competitor capacity fading price from late 2027, hyperscaler financing acting on orders with a 12-24 month lag, metals and currency), so I sit just below Arteche's enacted, funded grid demand and well above RELX, a touch above the group's 80.

2Internal change forces: a real operating reset, and a capital-allocation pattern that has not changed

The internal picture splits cleanly in two. The operating reset under the new team is real, measurable and running ahead of plan. The capital-allocation pattern of expensive, debt- and share-funded acquisitions has not changed, and it is the main reason the market applies a discount.

Evidence, positive: a new insider team. The board removed chief executive Peter Herweck in November 2024, after 18 months, for "divergences in executing the strategic roadmap". It appointed Olivier Blum, a 31-year insider who had run Energy Management, where revenue rose from EUR 26.4bn to EUR 31.1bn in two years and the margin rose 170 basis points to 22.1%. A new chief financial officer (Nathan Fast, April 2026) and a new head of investor relations (June 2026) followed, both internal appointments.

Evidence, positive: a numeric 2030 framework, with about half the five-year margin target delivered in year one. The December 2025 Capital Markets Day set the targets below, and the first year's evidence is already strong.

Evidence, positive: pricing, organisation and capacity. A new pricing methodology from 1 January 2026 took product price realisation to 5.1% by Q3 2026, against just above 2% at ABB and about 3% at Legrand. The Multi-Hub 2.0 programme is removing management layers by reorganising the group into four regions. Prefabrication capacity has grown fourfold to 1.35 million square feet on eight sites plus 12 partner sites, and Foxconn is adding asset-light North American capacity.

The insight the self-help narrative misses: the overhead gain is a freeze outgrown by revenue, not a cut. Schneider's absolute support-function costs are still rising, from EUR 7,859m in 2022 to EUR 9,375m in 2025, and by a further 4.9% in H1 2026, to EUR 4,921m for the half. The support-function ratio fell from 24.3% to 23.2% only because revenue grew 9.8%. The H1 2026 cost bridge shows gross savings of EUR 182m, against EUR 160m of reinvestment and EUR 129m of inflation. The support-cost base had grown 24% in three years (against 1% to 7% at peers), and freezing it improves the ratio only while revenue grows faster than about 5% a year. That condition is comfortably met at 10% growth, but it is also why a growth shock would become a margin shock before any real restructuring started.

Evidence, negative: about EUR 31bn to 32bn of acquisitions committed in twenty months, at top-of-market prices.

PTC contradicts management's own words. Schneider announced PTC ten months after management said acquisitions were "not a prerequisite" for its targets.

PTC's cost synergies are credible; its revenue synergies are not. Cost synergies of EUR 250m by year three are credible, and the savings from delisting PTC and from procurement make about half of them near-certain. The EUR 800m of revenue synergies (33% of PTC's sales) have no precedent at that scale, and Bernstein's bottom-up cross-selling analysis finds only about EUR 292m.

The funding dilutes shareholders and stops the buyback. Schneider placed 25m shares at EUR 240 (4.3% of its capital, at the low end of its five-year valuation range), issued a EUR 6bn bond at an average 4.3% with about EUR 10bn still to issue, takes leverage to about 2.3x in 2027, and has paused the buyback in 2027 and 2028.

Incentives and reported returns do not police capital allocation. The long-term incentive plan (40% adjusted EPS, 35% relative total shareholder return, 25% carbon) has no return-on-capital test, and the company's stated ROCE excludes EUR 10.2bn of minority buyouts, which are worth about 3 points of ROCE.

The software integration is under-staffed. Voluntary staff turnover has risen to 13.9%, with a "significant" loss of software and AI talent. Meanwhile three software platforms (AVEVA, Cognite and PTC) are to be unified at once by a leadership team with no external software operator in its top roles.

Inference and so-what. The split tells us how to forecast. Model operating profit on the strong forces, because the reset is real, measurable and ahead of plan. Model EPS and the balance sheet with the financing drag. Give no credit to revenue synergies or to multiple expansion until integration evidence exists. The operating reset is the most reliable driver of 2026 and 2027 earnings; capital allocation is the main reason the market applies a discount.

Counter-case. PTC may prove a sound deal by 2030. Redburn finds that excluding all PTC synergies cuts its DCF value by only 1%; Motivair is ahead of its business case; the software assets were bought during the "SaaS-pocalypse" de-rating of software-as-a-service stocks; and a 40%-margin software business mechanically lifts the group margin by 90 to 100 basis points. Even so, PTC is not a 2027 or 2028 earnings event.

What would change my view. On the positive side: evidence of an absolute reduction in support costs (not just a falling ratio) in the February 2027 cost bridge; a dated PTC revenue-synergy plan; or the appointment of an external software leader. On the negative side: a second acquisition-driven capital raise.

Versus the market. The market has the deal verdict right ("great operator, bad deal") and is right to doubt the synergies. It has not yet put the deal's 2027 per-share mechanics into its numbers, and it reads the overhead gain as cost discipline when it is growth leverage.

Conclusion: the internal change is a genuine, measurable operating turnaround inside a growing business, offset but not cancelled by the heaviest and most expensive acquisition programme in the sector and an incentive system that does not police it.

Score: 65, set by the Rater. The operating reset under an insider CEO is real and in the numbers (half the five-year margin plan in year one, product price 5.1% against peers' 2-3%, productivity of EUR 535m in one half, record free cash flow), but the overhead gain is a freeze outgrown by revenue, not a cut, and it is offset by EUR 31-32bn of top-of-market acquisitions (PTC at about 4% year-one ROCE), 4.3% dilution, leverage to 2.3x, a buyback pause and incentives with no return test, which take 6-7% off FY2027 EPS. A clear but offset positive, in line with the group's 63, between OEM's active acquirer and Teqnion's working clean-up.

3Structure, moat, financial profile and management

Industry structure: Schneider's profitable markets are concentrated, certification-gated oligopolies. The top three suppliers (Schneider, Vertiv and Delta) hold about 80% of data-centre power and cooling; the top five supply about 70% of critical data-centre electrical components; and the top five in busbar hold about 64%.

Customers rarely switch suppliers. Installed electrical systems last more than 20 years and are serviced through about 400 service centres. Hyperscale designers prefer proven brands because downtime penalties are severe. Certifications take six to 24 months, and utilities run one-year qualification tests.

Competitors put margin first. Legrand has never cut average prices in twenty years; ABB ties about half of its line managers' bonuses to local margin and uses ROCE in its incentives; and Eaton runs capacity discipline. No Western low-voltage list-price cuts occurred in 2009, 2016, 2020 or the 2023 to 2025 destocking.

The structure is fragile in two dated places, and little of Schneider's profit sits in either. The first is the scarcity premium, which competitor capacity erodes from 2027 to 2029. The second is the standardised low end, where new entrants have taken share fast: Chinese domestic brands hold 59% of servo motors and 61% of robots sold in China, Korean makers supply 19% of US transformer imports, and Indian transformer prices fell 25% to 30% when second-tier capacity arrived.

Competitive advantage: the moat is specification and switching costs, not a network effect. Schneider's moat has four parts: specification by designers and the switching costs of its installed base; regional manufacturing scale (about 90% of products are made in the region where they are sold, which is why tariffs cost Schneider only EUR 104m net in H1 2026 while Legrand imports 45% of its US cost base); certified prefabrication capacity; and the broadest integrated portfolio in the industry (low and medium voltage, secure power, cooling, building, grid and industrial software).

Customers now pay for exactly that combination: a delivery date and single-source integration at gigawatt scale. Schneider represents more than 20% of power spend for 64% of surveyed data-centre procurement managers, against 36% for Vertiv. Schneider sits in the NVIDIA DSX POD and AMD Helios reference designs. Compass (USD 3bn over five years) and Switch (USD 1.9bn) have signed capacity agreements with Schneider, and one operator moved its complex equipment from Legrand to Schneider.

The moat is narrowing in three places. Vertiv leads liquid cooling with over 20% share, with Schneider just under; traditional UPS faces 800-volt DC power after 2029; and Schneider lacks scale in automation software (Siemens' annual recurring revenue is EUR 5.7bn, against about EUR 3.5bn for Schneider pro forma after PTC). Eaton (Boyd, Fibrebond and about USD 11bn of deals) and Vertiv (UtilityInnovation) are buying the same integrated stack, which validates Schneider's architecture now and erodes its uniqueness later.

Financial profile: asset-light, cash-generative and high-margin, but with mediocre returns on total capital.

The margin gap to peers is also the catch-up reservoir. Energy Management gained only 430 basis points of margin from 2019 to 2024, against 990 at ABB and 730 at Eaton.

Management: strong operators, weak capital allocators. Schneider has a deep, stable, insider bench that is out-executing European peers on growth (Q3 2026 organic growth of 16.9%, against 14% at ABB and about 10.7% at Legrand) and on pricing, with the best margin bridge in the peer group. The chief executive's record is one of operating delivery ("speed over perfection"; a "pushy executor" in the Leadership digest's terms).

Management's weaknesses are concentrated in capital allocation. Schneider has been a net issuer of shares since 2019 (551m to 562m shares even before the placement), and it paused buybacks near a valuation low. Incentives carry no return test, management's communication about capital allocation has been at odds with its actions, and the team is thin in software just as software becomes the riskiest leg of the strategy. Governance scaffolding is above French norms (a 92% independent board, separate chair and chief executive roles, and a clawback since 2023), but shareholders do not come first in capital allocation.

Inference and so-what. Mechanical forces will improve Energy Management's results for four years without heroics: backlog repricing, a fixed overhead base, the end in 2026 of the drag from AVEVA's transition to subscriptions, a growing installed base, and SF6-replacement demand set by law. Energy Management's margin path to about 24% by 2030 can therefore be forecast with reasonable confidence. The heroic parts of the plan (integrating PTC and Cognite, lifting Industrial Automation's margin from 14% to 18%, and lifting AVEVA's from 17% to 30%) deserve the haircuts the model gives them. Precedent in this sector rewards secular exposure, self-help and disciplined capital allocation together. Schneider has two of the three, which is why its shares follow the underperformance pattern while its earnings follow the outperformance pattern, and why a re-rating needs integration proof or a return to buybacks, not just earnings beats.

Energy Management is about 83% of revenue and carries most of the consensus growth, from EUR 33.1bn in FY2025 to EUR 47.1bn in FY2028.

Counter-case. Schneider's specification lead may be worth less after 2028 than it is in today's scarcity. Industry experts describe Schneider as the most growth-first of the majors, occasionally pricing aggressively on large data-centre tenders to win the lifecycle service tail. Hyperscalers select from three or four qualified suppliers per category and "squeeze hardware margins to single digits" in negotiation, so a renegotiation after 2028 could compress the premium.

What would change my view. Loss of specification share in the next Bernstein survey; Vertiv or Eaton winning hyperscale single-source campus awards for which Schneider was specified; or an Energy Management margin below 23% in FY2026 despite the volume.

Versus the market. I agree with the market on the moat and the margin gap; my difference is one of emphasis. The market values Schneider's industrial automation and software at close to zero (Jefferies estimates zero to eight times operating profit) while applying a sector-level discount to the hardware franchise. That leaves a gap between the share price and the quality of the franchise that delivery can close.

Conclusion: a top-two franchise in a concentrated, margin-first industry with a widening delivery moat and an above-average operating profile, run by strong operators whose capital allocation is the one below-average foundation.

Score: 73, set by the Rater. Qualitatively strong: a top-two position in concentrated, certification-gated, margin-first oligopolies, a widening specification, regional-scale and prefabrication moat, and margins that held in 2009 and 2020, so predictability is high; ROIC of 10% (66th percentile) and margins at the 58th-64th percentiles understate an asset-light model earning 25-30% on new organic capital. But return on new invested capital overall is poor, with about EUR 31bn deployed at low returns (PTC about 4%, the Indian minority about 2.5%) and management's capital allocation below average, so with the groups at 75/72/62/54 it sits just below Tenaris and above Volex.

4Guidance conservatism, expectation management and the record of delivery

Schneider's initial annual guidance has been a floor in each of the last three years. The 2024 organic guide of 6% to 8% was tracked. The 2025 guide of 7% to 10% delivered 8.9%, with the margin at the bottom of its range because of currency. The 2026 guide was set at 7% to 10% in February and held at Q1 despite an 11.2% print (Deutsche Bank called it "highly conservative"); it was then raised to 10% to 13% in July and to 12% to 14% in October, while the margin guide moved from +50 to 80 basis points to +100 to 120 basis points (a 19.7% to 19.9% margin).

Every 2026 print beat expectations. Q1 organic growth was 11.2% against 10.1% expected; Q2 was 16.5% against 10.6%; the H1 margin was 19.3% against 18.5%; productivity was EUR 272m above expectations; free cash flow was 17% above; and Q3 revenue was 3% above.

The FY2026 guide is still mildly sandbagged. At its midpoint the FY2026 guide implies about 8% organic growth in Q4, after about 15% in the first nine months, even though the backlog is at a record and product growth is accelerating; and management's bonus targets are already exceeded. Consensus FY2026 EBIT margin (18.8%, about 19.7% on an adjusted EBITA basis once amortisation is added back) sits at the bottom of the guided margin range.

Informal commentary runs above the formal guide. Management speaks of "visibility into 2028", "absolute confidence" in the 250 basis points of margin gain "across all economic growth scenarios", and a strategy "at halftime".

Two statements carry credibility risk. The one informal statement contradicted by action was "M&A is not a prerequisite". The one piece of guidance that will need reconciling is that PTC will be "immediately low-single-digit accretive": that claim is true on a full-year pro forma basis and false for FY2027 as it will be reported.

The longer record: operations deliver, but reported EPS repeatedly lands below earlier expectations. Organic growth guidance has been met or beaten for three years. Reported EPS, however, keeps falling short because of what sits between operating profit and the share: FY2025 EPS consensus once stood at EUR 9.77 and the outcome was EUR 8.59 (currency and interest), and FY2026 consensus fell from EUR 11.10 to EUR 9.75 before recovering to EUR 10.33. In 2020, when revenue fell 7.4%, the margin held.

Revenue growth accelerated to +9.8% in H1 2026 and the EBITDA margin reached 22.2%, the highest of the eleven half-years.

Inference and so-what: the guidance pattern to expect through 2027.

  1. 18 February 2027: FY2026 lands at the top of its ranges (about 75% probability of the top half; 10% probability of landing above the range).
  2. 18 February 2027: an initial FY2027 organic guide with a midpoint of 8% to 9.5% (the framework is 7% to 10%) and a margin guide of +50 to 80 basis points. That guide will sit below what the business can do and below the 9.5% to 10.5% organic growth that consensus implies, and it carries a headline risk if it is read against a reported-basis consensus that already includes acquisitions.
  3. Late July 2027: a raise at the half-year (about 65% probability), when the price carry-over peaks.
  4. Q3 2027: a reaffirmation or narrowing of guidance alongside the PTC closing.

For forecasting, lean to the top of guidance on organic growth and margin (we sit at 13.9% and 19.9% for FY2026), and lean neutral to down on EPS and on anything that depends on a buyback.

Counter-case. If the market has fully learnt Schneider's low-ball pattern, guidance raises stop moving the shares (Jefferies' point in January 2025), and a February guide at the framework could be read as the first sign of deceleration rather than as prudence. Deutsche Bank expects the initial FY2027 margin guide to be only +50 basis points.

What would change my view. An initial FY2027 guide with a midpoint at or above 10% organic growth (upside confirmed early); a Q4 2026 organic print below 8% (the sandbag was not a sandbag); or H2 2026 net price near zero rather than the +EUR 150m that management has implied.

Versus the market. The sell-side knows Schneider's guidance habit and prices a raise. It has not priced the credibility test on the PTC accretion claim, nor the risk on 18 February 2027 that an organic guide is compared with a reported-basis consensus. I weight both risks more than the market does, which is why the February event is two-sided for the shares even though it is one-sided for the operating evidence.

Conclusion: guidance is conservative, specific and habitually raised at the half-year, consensus sits at the bottom of the margin range, and the only credibility risk lies below the operating line, in the PTC accretion language.

Score: 72, set by the Rater. Operating guidance has been a floor for three years: 2026 raised twice with every print beating, the Q4 guide implying about 8% organic after 15%, and consensus margin at the bottom of the range, so current guidance is conservative. Held back by a short record under the new team, reported EPS repeatedly landing below earlier expectations (FY2025 EUR 9.77 to 8.59), and two credibility marks ('M&A is not a prerequisite' contradicted by PTC; the 'immediately accretive' claim false for FY2027 as reported), coherent with the groups' 70 and 45; just below Kerry's consistent delivery.

5Why revenue growth turns into outsized profit growth, and why it turns into less EPS growth than that

The transmission in one line. In FY2027, revenue growth of 12.6% becomes adjusted EBITA growth of about 19% through price, productivity and a frozen overhead, but only 14.9% EPS growth, because the new shares and the acquisition interest absorb four to five points.

Pricing power is demonstrated, and its real gain comes in 2027. Schneider raised product prices by 5.1% by Q3 2026 while orders rose and its specification share held. Indexation clauses let systems contracts reprice the backlog; low-voltage content is only 6% to 7% of a project's construction cost, so customers are not price-sensitive; and product list prices are sticky through downturns.

Pricing power has four limits. Direct list pricing touches less than half of sales; large tenders are competitive; the 2026 acceleration was mostly cost recovery (net price was −EUR 154m in H1 2026), so the real gain is the 2027 carry-over; and the competitor capacity wave fades price from about 2.5 points of growth in 2026 to about 1 point by 2029.

Operating leverage is moderate and asymmetric: strong on the way up, mild on the way down. On the way up, 2026 organic adjusted EBITA growth of 18% to 21% on revenue growth of 12% to 14% implies incremental margins of 27% to 30%, against an average margin of about 20%, because price, productivity and a frozen overhead compounded with volume. The leverage lives in the semi-fixed cost base (support functions about 23% of sales, R&D about 6%), and the overhead gap to Eaton (SG&A of 15.7% of sales) is the reservoir that the leverage drains.

On the way down, Schneider's decremental margins have historically been at or below its average margin. About 45% of revenue is purchased material, which is variable, and Schneider has flexed support costs fast in past downturns: it cut EUR 541m in 2009, when organic sales fell 15.7% and the margin fell only 310 basis points, and margins rose on flat or falling sales in 2016 and 2020. The range of FY2027 outcomes is therefore narrower for operating profit than for revenue: a five-point swing in FY2027 organic growth moves EBITA by about EUR 450m to 650m (5% to 7% of EPS), with the upper figure applying on the downside if prefabrication capacity is under-absorbed.

Cost-out is large in gross terms and small in net terms. In gross terms, productivity will beat the EUR 2bn to 2.5bn plan, and the support-function ratio should fall about 3 points from 2025 to 2030, against a target of 1.5 to 2 points. In net terms, H1 2026 productivity of EUR 535m lifted the gross margin by only 10 basis points, because it funded raw materials and tariffs; support savings fund reinvestment and inflation; and R&D rising to about 6.6% of sales gives back 0.7 points. Net, cost levers add about 0.4 points of margin a year from 2027 to 2030, plus PTC's EUR 250m of cost synergies (about 40 basis points by 2030).

Falling restructuring costs are a 2027 EPS tailwind that no broker frames. Restructuring costs fall from EUR 450m in 2026 to EUR 250m in 2027, which is worth about EUR 0.26 of FY2027 EPS.

Financial leverage works against EPS through 2028 and for it from 2029. Net financial items roughly double, from −EUR 715m in 2025 to −EUR 1,480m in 2028, to buy a 4%-return asset, with 4.3% more shares and no buyback. From 2029, deleveraging and a buyback of EUR 1.1bn and then EUR 1.3bn turn financial leverage into a tailwind of about 2 points of EPS growth a year.

Reinforcing feedback loops run through 2027.

  • Prefabrication wins share. Prefabrication cuts on-site installation work by about 80%. That drives single-sourcing, which lifts content per megawatt (prefabricated electrical rooms carry USD 1.8m to 2.8m per MW) and share, which funds more capacity; modular builds are projected to rise from 20% to 60% of builds by 2030.
  • Volume funds investment. Volume leverage on the frozen overhead funds R&D and capacity.
  • Old contracts roll off. Systems margins keep rising into 2028 as lower-margin backlog signed before 2022 ships.
  • Reference designs raise specification share. Inclusion in NVIDIA and AMD reference designs makes Schneider a gatekeeper.
  • The installed base feeds services and software. Services are worth up to about 10% of data-centre capex, and PTC adds EUR 2.4bn of annual recurring revenue that is 96% recurring.

Balancing feedback loops are building, and they bite from H2 2027 to 2029. Scarcity pricing invites competitor capacity (bites from H2 2027 to 2029). Debt-financed demand invites wider credit spreads (latent, and the swing factor). Load growth invites permit brakes (a timing effect, partly self-cancelling through higher behind-the-meter content). High margins invite entrants in standard products (contained).

The reinforcing loops carry 2026 and 2027; the balancing loops bite from H2 2027 to 2029, which is why 2028 is the more fragile year.

The arithmetic of transmission from FY2026 to FY2027 (model). Three to four points of operating growth are lost to the share count, and about one point to interest and tax. In 2026 the gearing ran the other way (EPS +19% on revenue +13%), helped by the removal of the Indian minority, which was worth about +1 point net of its funding cost.

Inference and so-what. For the next two years, 10% organic growth at Schneider becomes 15% to 19% operating profit growth through mechanisms that are already visible. The leakage from operating profit to each share is a financing choice, not a business flaw: the quality of EPS growth is high (it is organic, with no buyback), but its quantity in 2027 is lower than the operating momentum suggests. The "contracted margin" effect described in the Industry Digest means systems margins keep rising into 2028 even as list-price momentum fades, which is why the FY2028 margin can still exceed FY2027's despite the capacity wave.

Counter-case. The reinforcing loops depend on growth. If revenue growth falls below about 5%, the overhead ratio stops falling and real cuts, with their restructuring costs, become necessary. And once scarcity ends, hyperscalers will renegotiate framework pricing; their capacity-reservation agreements often carry no binding minimum volumes.

What would change my view. Distributor surveys showing fewer than 50% of distributors receiving supplier price increases; product price realisation below 2% in Q3 2027; or a half-year in which support costs grow faster than revenue.

Versus the market. The sell-side models the leverage, but it under-weights three things: the dependence of the overhead gain on growth, the dated nature of the backlog repricing, and the fall in restructuring costs. On balance, those three net to a modestly better 2027 margin and a more fragile 2028 than consensus carries.

Conclusion: revenue growth turns into roughly double that rate of operating profit growth through price carry-over, overhead leverage and backlog repricing, and into about 1.2 times that rate of EPS growth in 2027 and 2028 because PTC's financing absorbs the rest.

Score: 65, set by the Rater. Pricing power is proven (5.1% product price without share loss, low price elasticity, sticky list prices) and 2026 incremental margins of 27-30% come from a semi-fixed base of about 29% of sales (support functions 23%, R&D 6%) plus reinforcing prefabrication and installed-base loops, but about 45% of revenue is variable purchased material, so operating gearing is moderate (operating profit about twice revenue growth) and mild on the way down. Financial leverage works against EPS through 2028 (net financial items doubling, 4.3% more shares), so forecast EPS grows only about 1.4 times revenue, below the median's 2; strong on price and loops, ordinary on gearing, coherent with the groups' 62 and 60.

Conclusion: the forecasts give double-digit revenue growth to 2028, margins 300 to 400 basis points above the past and a 15% EPS CAGR, with operating lines at or above consensus and EPS 6 to 7% below it for reasons that are facts rather than views.

Score: 90, set by the Rater. About 15.4% sits just inside the A band (15-30%); I place it at the floor because the rate decelerates (19%, 15%, 15%, 12.5%), FY2026 carries about a point from the Indian minority buyout, and from FY2026's base the forward rate is about 13.6%. Against that the growth is organic and the margin path (adjusted EBITA 18.7% to 22.3%) runs well above the past, which keeps it in A rather than B.

7Scope for upgrades over the next six to twelve months: operating lines up, EPS down first

The key point for the next six months. A negative EPS revision in the December 2026 or February 2027 consensus collection will be an accounting catch-up on the share count and coupon, not an operating signal.

Consensus operating lines have room to rise. Consensus FY2026 EBITDA is 1.7% below ours, and its margin sits at the bottom of the guided range. FY2027 EBITDA consensus is in line with ours, and FY2028 EBITDA consensus is 3.7% below ours, partly because some broker models do not carry a full year of PTC.

Consensus EPS has not yet absorbed the PTC financing. Almost all of the 21 FY2027 EPS estimates that FactSet holds are dated 16 to 20 October 2026, before the placement was sized (21 October) and the bond priced (28 October). Bernstein carries a flat 577m share count and net interest of EUR 466m in 2027, about EUR 1bn below our 2028 financing line; Redburn models 22m new shares at a 3.5% coupon. The AlphaSense audit of broker models lists UBS, Goldman, Barclays, Berenberg, RBC, Santander, Morgan Stanley and others as not yet integrating the share count or coupon. Deutsche Bank itself says consensus "updates are highly staggered" and the aggregate "remains overstated".

Broker FY2027 EPS spans EUR 10.65 to 13.67 because most brokers have not yet built in the new shares and the coupon.

The sequence I expect: EPS consensus drifts down first, and operating upgrades follow in February and July 2027. The timeline below sets out each step. Three details sit behind it. In February 2027, FY2026 EPS should be in line (consensus EUR 10.30, against our EUR 10.3 to 10.4), while FY2028 EPS falls 1% to 3% as brokers rebuild their interest lines. In October 2027, the FY2028 rebase on the audited purchase-price allocation and integration costs (EUR 250m of implementation cost) is most likely to be −1% to −2%; in the Altair precedent, consensus mis-modelled EUR 150m of such costs at Siemens. By end-2027, FY2027 EPS consensus should be about EUR 12.0 to 12.2 (against EUR 12.61 today and our EUR 11.76), and FY2028 about EUR 13.8 to 14.0 (against EUR 14.49 today and our EUR 13.51).

EPS consensus drifts down first and operating upgrades follow in February and July 2027: the window in which both turn together opens between those two results.

The narrative can improve on delivery rather than on surprise. The first steps of the sequence remove negatives: the equity overhang is already gone; the pending deals close; the FY2026 margin is confirmed; the FY2027 guide is set; and the year-end backlog is disclosed. The backlog is published only annually, and it is the single most useful number for 2027. The novel positives sit in months 6 to 36: PTC's first combined plan, margin progress at Industrial Automation and AVEVA, the content gain from hybrid 800-volt architecture, a possible upgrade of the 2030 framework after FY2027, and the 2029 buyback restart.

Mid-term targets: the margin and data-centre targets are more likely to be beaten than met; the return and buyback targets are at risk. The +250 basis points of margin and the 12% to 14% data-centre CAGR are more likely to be beaten than met. The ROCE ambition of 15% to 20% will be missed in substance once PTC's capital is counted. The buyback is the commitment with the least slack.

Inference and so-what. Over the next six months, the gap between our assessment and the market is favourable on what Schneider will report and unfavourable on what the market is counting. The two reconcile during 2027, with the EPS drift first and the operating upgrades second. A "negative EPS revision" print in December or February is therefore not an operating signal, and this memo should say so before the dashboard shows it to the market.

Counter-case. The EPS drift could be masked. If brokers update share counts and coupons in the same note in which they raise operating estimates after a strong February, the headline revision series could stay positive. And if the FY2027 organic guide is set above 10%, FY2027 EBITDA upgrades could be 4% to 5% rather than 1% to 3%.

What would change my view. A February guide at the framework midpoint, with margin at +50 basis points and a backlog growing below 10%, would remove the upgrade scope. A year-end backlog above +15% with net price above +EUR 150m would make the upgrade scope larger and earlier.

Versus the market. The market expects "beat and raise". I expect "beat on operations, drift on EPS, raise in July", which is less tidy and, for the first two consensus collections, worse.

Conclusion: operating estimates should rise 1% to 3% for 2027 and 3% to 5% for 2028 over the next twelve months, but EPS consensus falls 3% to 5% first, so the upgrade story reaches the headline numbers only from July 2027.

Score: 46, set by the Rater. Guidance, which counts most, is likely set low in February (organic midpoint 8-9.5% against the 9.5-10.5% consensus implies) and then raised in July 2027 (about 65%), a positive on operating lines; but consensus FY2027 EPS, the line that drives the price, is likely to fall about 3-5% net by end-2027 as share count and coupon are absorbed, about -0.3 to -0.45 times 11% revenue growth (roughly the 30th percentile), with EBITDA only +1-3%. The narrative improves mainly after month 6, so net scope is slightly negative, coherent with the group's 52 less the EPS drift; between Kerry and Carlsberg.

8Momentum now: estimates up, price and narrative down, and the same split across the sector

Estimate momentum is strong: FY2027 consensus has risen on every line over every period. Guidance was raised twice in 2026, the dashboard's revision-momentum score is 7, and its sell-side earnings momentum letter is B (snapshot of 24 October 2026).

Ratings and targets are moving the other way. The mean target price fell 2% in a month, to EUR 328.68 (42% above the share price), and the share of buy ratings fell 7 points in a month, to 65%. The Wisdom Library calls this a "ratings against revisions" divergence: it means the debate has moved from earnings to capital allocation and valuation.

Narrative momentum is negative: "great operator, bad deal". The sell-side's coverage is complete on the sector stories (AI financing, the 2028 pricing fade, the buyback pause and doubtful synergies). It is incomplete on the mechanics that will decide FY2027 EPS: the share count set against only one quarter of PTC profit, the coupon, the dependence of the overhead gain on growth, and the fall in restructuring costs. The software weighting imports the "SaaS-pocalypse" frame from software stocks.

Buy-side evidence is thin but not hostile. In Jefferies' survey 60% of investors intended to keep an overweight position; some active managers trimmed on the deal; 55% of European long-only funds were overweight before it; short interest is near zero; and there is no activist, partly because voting caps of 10% to 15% raise the cost of one.

Technical momentum is weak (grade D at 24 October 2026), but less weak than the sector's. The price is 13.3% below its 200-day average, relative strength is at the 22nd percentile of the universe, and the price is down 11.7% over three months and 8.2% over twelve, although the 200-day average was rising in 11 of the last 12 months. Schneider's six-month correlation with the sector basket is 0.71 (R-squared 51%, down from 66% to 69% before PTC), and over six months Schneider (−8.4%) has outperformed the basket (−11.3%). Thematic Fit/Momentum is D. The Fitness for Fighting regime is risk-off, with Momentum at Underweight, Fragility at Double Underweight and France at Double Underweight.

Peers show the same split between estimates and price. Sell-side earnings momentum is A at ABB, Legrand, Siemens Energy, Prysmian and NKT, while technical momentum is D or F at all 16 sector stocks. Twelve-month share-price returns are ABB +17.6%, Siemens Energy +14.8%, Prysmian +11.0%, Siemens +7.7% and Legrand −15.4%.

Raising targets within a year of setting them is now the sector habit, and it has not protected multiples. Legrand raised its targets in September 2026 to 6% to 8% growth and a 21% to 22% margin, and its forward multiple still contracted about 15% with the sector; Vertiv, Eaton, Siemens Energy and ABB all raised frameworks in the last two years. Peers' results also show the beat-on-operations, miss-on-EPS pattern being punished in the short run: ABB's Q3 2026 EPS missed by 18% on a non-cash hedge loss, and Morgan Stanley cut its ABB target multiple from 20.6x to 18.5x on peer de-rating.

The whole sector shares the price weakness, and Schneider has held up better than its basket.

Inference and so-what. Estimate momentum is strong and real; price and narrative momentum are weak and mostly sector-driven. The dashboard's valuation letter D (77th percentile) rests on a trailing P/E of 21.3x that the earnings inflection has made stale. The near-term risk to Schneider's momentum picture is the EPS consensus drift described in #7, which could move the sell-side letter from B to C without any operating news. The near-term support is that the sector's own momentum is uniformly weak, so Schneider's relative position cannot get much worse on that measure. Precedent says that a de-rating on a technology or financing narrative persists until the company reframes its exposure (Legrand's took a year and a Capital Markets Day); Schneider's reframing events are the February and July 2027 results.

Counter-case. Momentum investors will not own a stock 13% below its 200-day average with a falling share of buy ratings, and the December consensus collection will give them a reason to stay away. A technical turn needs the price back above about EUR 267, the 200-day average, which is 15% higher.

What would change my view. On the positive side: a positive EPS revision month after the December collection (the drift was smaller than feared), or the sector's technical letters improving as AI credit stabilises. On the negative side: the share of buy ratings falling below 55%.

Versus the market. I agree that price momentum is poor. I differ in attributing most of it to the sector and the deal rather than to Schneider's earnings, and in expecting the estimate series to split (EBITDA up, EPS down) rather than move together.

Conclusion: momentum is strongly positive in guidance and operating estimates, negative in price, ratings and narrative, and about to look worse in headline EPS revisions before July 2027, with the whole sector sharing the price weakness.

Score: 56, set by the Rater. One positive and one negative measure gives C. Guidance raised twice and FY2027 EPS up 7% over three months and 9% over six (82nd percentile) lean positive, while the buy share fell 7 points, targets edged down, the narrative is 'great operator, bad deal' and the price is 13% below its 200-day average, with peers strong on estimates but D/F technically everywhere, so I place it in the lower-middle of the band.

9Riskiness and simplicity of the case

The case is concentrated, not diffuse, which makes it easier to track. It has one dominant operating driver: data-centre conversion, roughly half of 2026 and 2027 organic growth and about EUR 1.3bn of the EUR 3.0bn increase in EBITA from 2025 to 2027. It has two medium operating drivers (net price-cost in 2027, and overhead leverage), two large known negatives below the operating line (the new shares and interest), and one bounded unknown (the PTC closing date). That structure is easier to track than the 2019 to 2025 period, when several medium drivers (currency, interest, acquisitions and four end markets) offset one another and made EPS unpredictable.

The cost of concentration is exposure to one external variable that Schneider does not disclose: the financing of marginal data-centre demand.

Fragilities and requirements: FY2027 rests on demonstrated levers; from 2028 the forecast shifts to undemonstrated ones.

The FY2027 forecast requires

  • Backlog conversion at or near the 2026 pace (booked)
  • Product price carry-over against plateauing metals (contractual on price, open on cost)
  • Revenue growth above about 5%, to keep the overhead ratio falling (comfortable in 2027)
  • Acquisition debt at about 4.6%
  • PTC closing on 1 October 2027

The FY2027 forecast does not require

  • Revenue synergies
  • Removal of overhead costs
  • An 18% Industrial Automation margin
  • A share buyback

From 2028 the forecast depends increasingly on the undemonstrated strengths (PTC integration, Industrial Automation and AVEVA), while the demonstrated lever, overhead leverage, weakens as growth normalises. That shift is why the range of FY2028 EPS outcomes is about twice as wide as FY2027's.

Sudden and material risks over 18 months: the operating risks are low to medium in plausibility; the sentiment risks are high and partly realised.

Sector precedents: the multiple moves first, and deep estimate cuts come only with capital-spending freezes. Capital-goods consensus EPS was cut about 40% in 2002 to 2003 and in 2008 to 2009, and by 15% to 20% in the milder slowdowns of 2011 to 2012 and 2015 to 2016. The sector multiple de-rated 29% in 2012 to 2013 and 33% at the start of the pandemic before estimates moved. The deep cuts came with capital-spending freezes, not with normalisations.

Schneider's own downturn record is mild. In 2009 organic growth was −15.7% and the margin fell 310 basis points; in 2020 organic growth was −4.7% and the margin rose 20 basis points.

Data-centre order surges have paused before, but revenue rarely falls within 18 months of a surge. Data-centre orders paused within 18 months of a surge at Marvell in 2017 to 2018, and Vertiv's orders went from flat to +13% to above +100% within 18 months. Revenue declines within 18 months of a surge are rare because of the conversion lag. Today's cycle has a buffer those precedents lacked (a record backlog described as seven to eight months of cushion, and two-to-three-year hyperscaler commitments) and a fragility they also lacked (debt-financed demand at the margin).

Trackability: Schneider's own disclosure confirms delivery after the fact and cannot anticipate a turn. Schneider discloses margins twice a year and the backlog once a year, with no quarterly orders or book-to-bill. Between now and April 2027 there are only two company data points (18 February and late April). The drivers that matter most are tracked externally, through the indicators in the panel below, through the coupon and currency of the remaining EUR 10bn of debt, and through the PTC proxy statement and the US antitrust (Hart-Scott-Rodino, HSR) and foreign-investment (CFIUS) filings. The merger agreement's drop-dead date of 4 April 2027 extends automatically in three-month steps up to nine months, and the AVEVA and OSIsoft precedent shows that a CFIUS review can add a quarter.

The one risk that turns deceleration into decline shows first in credit spreads and peer order prints, never in Schneider's own disclosure.

Inference and so-what. Over 18 months the case is predictable on revenue and adjusted EBITA (about 75% and 70% probability of landing within 5% of base), moderately predictable on EPS (about 60%), and it resolves on a known calendar. Its riskiness lies not in the operating forecast but in three other places: a per-share consensus that is 6 to 7% too high, a multiple set by a sector fear, and a 2028 in which four negatives land together. A plausible holding therefore has a cleaner first half and a murkier second. The Wisdom Library's rule applies to 2027: "pay for conversion once the orders are in; the first half of a one-to-two-year holding is the cleaner half".

Counter-case. Concentration in one theme that the market is actively repricing is exactly what makes a stock fall 26% while its estimates rise 11%, and the next such fall does not need an earnings miss.

What would change my view. If several of the external leading indicators above turned in the same direction at once in Q1 2027, the case would move from "predictable with a 2028 question" to "volatile now".

Versus the market. The market treats Schneider as an AI-infrastructure beta stock with a deal problem. I treat it as a concentrated but largely booked operating case with a per-share arithmetic problem that resolves within two consensus collections.

Conclusion: the case is simple in its drivers and predictable on operations for 18 months, moderately risky on EPS and the multiple, and carries one correlated, externally driven tail (data-centre financing) that would hit 2028 and is visible only through credit markets and peers.

Between the groups' 55 and 68, between OEM's narrow range and Shell's commodity exposure.

10Where the stock is in its lifecycle

The stock is Bottoming while the business is Reinforcing. The gap between the two phases is both the opportunity and the risk, and the dated path to a turn runs from the February 2027 results to the July 2027 results.

Evidence: the dashboard's rule puts the share price in the Bottoming phase. Technical momentum is D; the price is 26% off its high and 13% below its 200-day average; and the two-year-forward multiple has de-rated from about 21x in September 2026 (at a price of EUR 292) to about 18x on our EPS at EUR 231, while FY2027 estimates rose 7% over three months. A fresh company-specific discount for PTC (October 2026) sits on top of a sector de-rating, the share of buy ratings is falling, and target prices are edging down.

Evidence: the business is in peak delivery. Growth is running at nearly twice the company's normal rate, guidance has been raised twice, half the five-year margin plan was delivered in year one, and cash flow and the backlog are at records.

Inference: the turn up needs three conditions that are on the calendar, and a fourth that is not. The EPS consensus reset must run its course (December 2026 to February 2027); the February results must prove the backlog and set a credible FY2027 guide; and the July 2027 raise must restart positive EPS revisions. The fourth condition, an easing of the sector's financing fear, is not on Schneider's calendar.

My reading of the phase path. The bottom is most plausibly made between now and the February 2027 results, and "Turning Up" is the base case for H1 2027. The phase could move to "Thesis Broadening" if PTC's first combined plan and Industrial Automation margin progress arrive in H2 2027.

The recovery window is finite. From Q4 2027 the rates of change in data-centre growth, price and year-on-year comparisons turn against the stock, and 2028 is the year the debate becomes "how flat". A Reinforcing phase that starts in mid-2027 therefore has perhaps twelve to fifteen months before "Stalling" becomes the question. That limit is a reason to hold the phase judgement lightly and to treat 2027 as the cleaner year.

The stock is Bottoming while the business is Reinforcing; the dated path to Turning Up runs from the February to the July 2027 results.

In the sector's precedent, a stock bottoming on a capital-allocation controversy has also needed integration proof or buybacks to re-rate, and neither arrives at Schneider before 2028 to 2029.

What would change my view. The price regaining its 200-day average while the sector's technical letters improve would confirm the turn. Versus the market. The market broadly agrees that the stock is in a trough. My difference is the explicit calendar and the finite length of the recovery window, which argue for treating this as a 2027 phase rather than a multi-year re-rating.

Conclusion: Bottoming in price and multiple while Reinforcing in fundamentals, with a dated path to Turning Up between the February and July 2027 results and a recovery window that the 2028 normalisation debate will test within about a year of its start.

An attractive but conditional middle point, just above Greggs and below Nexans' paused Reinforcing.

11The fair multiple

Three "current multiple" readings circulate, and only one of them is current. On our EPS, Schneider trades at about 17.7 to 18.2 times two-year-forward earnings, almost exactly its ten-year median of 17.6x. The other two readings are stale in opposite directions.

FactSet's 16.33x is stale low. FactSet's 24-month-forward P/E (11th percentile of five years) divides the price by consensus EPS that has not absorbed the new shares. On our EPS the same measure is about 17.7x (the model's 18.2x uses its own blend of years), the 25th percentile of five years.

The dashboard's 21.3x is stale high. The dashboard's 21.3x (77th percentile of ten years, which drives the pinned valuation letter D) is a trailing current P/E, and the valuation-history page's "now 21.3x" dates from the September 2026 share price of EUR 292. The Phases page's statement that the guideline is "28% below the multiple now" therefore overstates the implied de-rating, which on our EPS is about 15% to 16%.

The ten-year bands span two regimes. The ten-year percentiles are 12.6x (10th), 15.3x (30th), 17.6x (median), 21.0x (75th) and 24.6x (90th). The 12x to 16x band is the 2016 to 2019 regime, when Schneider grew 5% to 6% with a 15% margin; the 17x to 23x band is the 2020 to 2026 regime.

Of the three current multiple readings only about 18x on Viewforth EPS is current, and it is the ten-year median, not a distressed multiple.

The guideline. Viewforth's rule for a Bottoming stock sets the fair multiple at the 30th percentile of the stock's own ten-year range, which for Schneider is 15.34x. The model's return in #12 uses that multiple.

My view: the guideline is the right floor, but a little too harsh as a central estimate for 18 months. The arguments on each side are set out below.

For a discount to the ten-year median

  • The stock is Bottoming, with an EPS consensus reset ahead.
  • Leverage rises to 2.3x and the buyback is paused until 2029; the 2016 to 2019 regime (near net cash, with buybacks) had neither.
  • The sector's multiple is set by an external financing fear; sector leaders trade at 14x to 20x on the dashboard's measure (Legrand 17.1x at its 8th percentile, Siemens Energy 14.4x, ABB 19.7x, Siemens 19.1x).
  • The software weighting imports a software discount.
  • A serial acquirer should arguably be valued after amortisation, which widens the gap between reported and adjusted EPS from 14% to about 18% from 2028.

For the median or above

  • The business now compounds EPS at about 15% a year, with margins above 20% and an A credit rating.
  • The drivers for the next 18 months are booked.
  • ABB re-rated to 28x to 33x forward earnings in its peak delivery phase, and Schneider's own five-year median is 20.4x.
  • Schneider has already outperformed its sector basket over six months, which suggests the company-specific discount is largely in the price.

Netting these arguments, I put the fair two-year-forward multiple at about 16.5x for the 18-month horizon (roughly the 40th percentile), and at the ten-year median of 17.6x for the three-year horizon. By the three-year horizon, deleveraging below 1.5x and the buyback restart should remove the two company-specific reasons for a discount. I would not use a multiple above the median in the base case until the 2028 normalisation debate has been had.

Counter-case. The 30th percentile may be the central case rather than the floor. If the market is right that electrical names should price a slowdown in data-centre spending (Morgan Stanley values some "at zero revenue growth in 2028"), the relevant comparison is a peer bear multiple near 15x EV/EBITA. And if per-share consensus falls 6% while the price holds, the forward multiple rises towards 19x without the stock moving, which would make today's price look less cheap in hindsight.

What would change my view. Upward: a credible PTC combined plan and the first evidence of Industrial Automation margin progress in H2 2027, or AI credit spreads normalising. Downward: a hyperscaler capex cut, or leverage still above 2x at end-2028.

Versus the market. The market's 16.3x screen rests on stale EPS, and its 21.3x trailing screen is stale in the other direction. Neither is the right number. About 17.7x to 18.2x is, and that is a median multiple for a top-quartile delivery year, not a distressed one.

Conclusion: the guideline 15.34x is a reasonable floor for a Bottoming stock with an EPS reset ahead, my central fair multiple is about 16.5x over 18 months and the ten-year median of 17.6x over three years, and the stock today trades at about 18x on our earnings, not the 16x or 21x the two screens suggest.

Score: 54, set by the Rater. Neutral on both gives C. The 77th percentile rests on a stale trailing P/E, and on the memo's EPS the forward multiple of about 18x sits at the ten-year median, but the peer reading leans dear and a Bottoming stock with leverage peaking and the buyback paused deserves less than its median (the memo's own fair multiple is about 16.5x), so I place it slightly above the floor of the band.

A plainer reconciliation of the 18-month return: earnings growth and de-rating cancel out, leaving the dividend. The split in the table is the model template's own. At end-2027 the model applies 15.34x to FY2029 EPS of EUR 15.21, which gives EUR 233 a share; adding EUR 10.2 of dividends (the FY2026 and FY2027 dividends of EUR 4.75 and EUR 5.40) gives EUR 243.40. Relative to today, two-year-forward EPS rolls forward about 20% (from EUR 12.7 to EUR 15.2), and the multiple falls about 16% (from 18.2x to 15.34x). Because 1.20 × 0.84 is about 1.01, the price is flat and the return is the dividend.

Over three years the earnings roll-forward wins. Two-year-forward EPS rolls forward about 39%, to about EUR 17.7 for the two years beyond mid-2029. The same 16% de-rating leaves +17% of price, and EUR 16.4 of dividends adds 7%, giving +24%.

Earnings do all the work. EPS compounding at about 15% a year is enough to absorb a de-rating to the 30th percentile and still return the cost of equity over three years. Dividends are a steady 2% to 2.5% a year (a payout ratio of about 45% to 46%, and progressive for 16 years).

The multiple is a drag at the guideline and the swing factor in every other case. Each turn of multiple is worth EUR 15 a share (6.6%) at December 2027 and about EUR 17.7 (7.6%) at June 2029. The grid below gives the return at each multiple. The 75th-percentile outcome (21.0x, +42% in 18 months) is the ABB-style peak-delivery outcome, not a base case.

Each turn of multiple is worth 6 to 8%: at the ten-year median the 18-month return is about +20%, at the 10th percentile on bear EPS about −27%.
